subject: SLA treatment for streaming vs sync endpoints - token throughput and TTF expectations
messages:
From: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@helioshealth.com>
To: evelyn_hart@redwood.ai
Cc: platform-ops@helioshealth.com
Date: 2026-11-28T15:12:00-08:00
Subject: Clarify streaming vs sync SLA terms (TTFT & token/sec)

Evelyn — thanks again for the demo today. Our security and platform teams are comfortable with Redwood overall, but procurement needs explicit language on how SLAs differ between streaming endpoints (server-sent, TTF-first-token expectations) and synchronous/batched endpoints.

Two asks from my side: 1) a short, ironclad definition of what's covered by the hosted SLA for time-to-first-token (TTFT) vs total response time on non-streaming endpoints, and 2) a clear numeric expectation for tokens/sec for streaming under the Dedicated plan (we need to map to our internal SLOs).

Can you send something we can include with our SOW? If Redwood has standard carveouts for high-token-rate burst traffic (e.g., spikes from batch inference), can you flag those too?

Cheers,
Alex Rivera
Director of Platform, Helios Health
---
Helios Health (secure)
From: evelyn_hart@redwood.ai
To: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@helioshealth.com>
Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.ai, markus_klein@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-11-28T17:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Clarify streaming vs sync SLA terms (TTFT & token/sec)

Alex — appreciate the clear asks. Quick summary of what I'll do and who I'm looping in:

- I attached a concise redline (Helios_SLA_Redlines_v2.pdf) with proposed wording around TTFT and per-token throughput for Dedicated.
- Looping in Markus (legal) and Laura (sales ops) to confirm we can commit to numeric expectations and list the carveouts.

High level answers for your procurement team to see now:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is defined as the elapsed time from accepted request at the Redwood edge until the first byte/token is delivered to the client stream; our hosted SLA target for TTFT on streaming endpoints under Standard tier is 200ms p50 and 450ms p95 for requests <1024 context tokens, measured at Redwood ingress.
- For non-streaming (sync/batched) endpoints the SLA covers service availability and request completion latency measured as request-to-last-byte; typical targets depend on model and batch size — we document model-level profiles in the catalog.
- Dedicated customers can elect a tokens-per-second floor per instance pool. For the Dedicated plan referenced in the SOW we propose a baseline of 120 tokens/sec sustained per GPU equivalent in the pool for models within the verified performance profile; bursts above that are handled by autoscaling or burst capacity but are excluded from the token-rate SLA.

Those numbers are starting points — Markus and Laura will follow up with precise contract language and carveout bullets (network outages, customer-side throttling, unusually long context lengths, and cold-cache windows).

If it's helpful, can you indicate the anticipated percent of traffic that will use streaming vs sync, and any expected 99th percentile token burst sizes? That will speed alignment.

Thanks,
Evelyn Hart
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
From: markus_klein@redwood.ai
To: evelyn_hart@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai
Cc: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@helioshealth.com>
Date: 2026-11-30T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Clarify streaming vs sync SLA terms (TTFT & token/sec)

Adding proposed contract language (high level) — see attached PDF for redlines. Key points I expect to include: 

1) Definition block: TTFT (time-to-first-token) = time from request acceptance at Redwood ingress to first token delivered to client (stream). We measure at egress to the client-facing TCP/TLS connection.

2) Numeric commitments (Dedicated): p50 TTFT <= 150ms and p95 TTFT <= 400ms for streaming on models within Redwood profile when requests are <1024 tokens and the pool is operating within its reserved capacity. Token throughput commitment: sustained baseline of 120 tokens/sec per GPU-equivalent; for customers requiring higher sustained throughput we will specify higher per-pool guarantees in the schedule.

3) Carveouts & credits: SLA credits apply only when the issue is within Redwood control (infrastructure, runtime). Carveouts include: upstream network failures, customer-origin traffic shaping, prolonged cold-starts caused by customer-driven model swaps, and traffic patterns with >10x baseline burst sustained longer than 60s that are outside agreed burst policies.

4) Streaming vs sync mapping: When a Customer uses our streaming API, TTFT language applies and token/sec commitments are relevant; when using sync/batched endpoints, SLA refers to request completion latency and throughput measured in requests/sec and average tokens per request.

Laura — can you confirm whether we should list a specific exception threshold for "burst windows" (60s vs 120s) in the SOW so Helios procurement has something concrete?

Markus Klein
Senior Counsel, Redwood Inference
From: Alex Rivera <alex.rivera@helioshealth.com>
To: evelyn_hart@redwood.ai
Cc: platform-ops@helioshealth.com, markus_klein@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai, rachel_kim@redwood.ai
Date: 2026-12-01T09:43:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Clarify streaming vs sync SLA terms (TTFT & token/sec)

Thanks — this is exactly what procurement needed. A couple quick clarifying notes from our ops team (copied):

- We prefer p95 TTFT as the primary contractual metric; p50 is great for engineering docs but not sufficient for contract enforcement.
- For dedicated baseline, Helios is open to the 120 tokens/sec per GPU-equivalent as a starting point, but we need an explicit test harness or reference benchmark (shared script or perf run) to validate that throughput against our model payloads. Can Redwood provide a short perf-run checklist or the benchmark harness used per-model?

We reviewed the redlines and will return comments on the carveout wording, but the numeric ranges look acceptable. If you can add a one-page appendix describing the validation run steps (endpoint, payload size, measurement method) that would unblock SOW sign-off.

Alex
Alex Rivera
Director of Platform, Helios Health
